questions.prompt: In what order does Python look up a name inside a nested function?
questions.explanation: The LEGB rule: the function's own local scope, then any enclosing function scopes, then the module's global scope, then built-ins.

sources.title: 4. Execution model — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: A name is resolved in the nearest enclosing scope: the local block, then enclosing function scopes, then the module's global namespace, and finally the builtins namespace.

questions.prompt: Given `x = 10` and `def f(): print(x); x = 5`, what happens when you call `f()`?
questions.explanation: Assigning to `x` anywhere in the function makes `x` local for the whole function body, which Python decides at compile time. The `print` reads the local `x` before it has been assigned.

sources.title: 4. Execution model — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: If a name is bound anywhere in a block, every use of it in that block refers to the local binding, and using it before it is bound in a function raises UnboundLocalError.

sources.title: Programming FAQ — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: The FAQ shows that assigning to `x` later in a function makes the compiler treat `x` as local, so an earlier `print(x)` raises UnboundLocalError.

questions.prompt: `def make_counter(): count = 0; def inc(): count += 1; return count; return inc`. What happens when you call `make_counter()()`?
questions.explanation: `count += 1` assigns to `count`, which makes it local to `inc`, and the local is read before it exists. Declaring `nonlocal count` inside `inc` makes the assignment rebind the enclosing variable instead.

sources.title: Programming FAQ — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: The FAQ's example shows `x += 1` inside a function makes `x` local, so reading it first raises UnboundLocalError even when an outer `x` exists.

sources.title: 7. Simple statements — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: `nonlocal` makes the listed names refer to bindings in the nearest enclosing function scope, allowing nested code to rebind them.

questions.prompt: What is a closure in Python, and what does `nonlocal` do?

model_answer.summary: A closure is an inner function that keeps access to variables from its enclosing function after that function has returned. `nonlocal` lets the inner function assign to those variables.
key_points: A closure is an inner function that refers to variables from an enclosing function's scope
Those captured variables stay alive after the outer function returns (they are stored in cells, visible through `__closure__`)
Without `nonlocal`, assigning to the name inside the inner function creates a new local variable
`nonlocal` makes the assignment rebind the variable in the enclosing scope

questions.explanation: Closures are how decorators, factories and callbacks carry state without a class. `nonlocal` is only needed when you rebind the variable. Mutating a captured list or dict works without it.

sources.title: 3. Data model — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: A function's `__closure__` is None or a tuple of cells holding the bindings of the function's free variables.

sources.title: 7. Simple statements — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: The `nonlocal` statement lets nested code rebind names bound in an enclosing function's scope.

sources.title: 4. Execution model — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: A name bound in a block is local to that block unless declared nonlocal or global, and a name used but not defined in a block is a free variable.

questions.prompt: What does `fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]; print([f() for f in fs])` print?
questions.explanation: Closures look up `i` when they are called, not when they are created. By the time any lambda runs, the loop has finished and `i` is 2.

sources.title: Programming FAQ — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: Lambdas created in a loop look up the loop variable when called, not when defined, so after the loop they all see its final value.

questions.prompt: Which version produces `[0, 1, 2]` when each function is called?

choices.text: `[lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]`

questions.explanation: A default argument is evaluated when the lambda is created, so `i=i` captures the current value on each loop iteration. `functools.partial` is another fix.

sources.title: Programming FAQ — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: Writing the lambda as `lambda n=x: ...` captures the loop value, because a default is computed when the lambda is defined.

questions.prompt: For `def f(a, /, b, *, c): ...`, which call is valid?
questions.explanation: `a` comes before `/`, so it is positional-only and can't be passed by name. `c` comes after `*`, so it is keyword-only and must be passed by name. `b` can be passed either way. `f(1, b=2)` fails because `c` is required.

sources.title: 8. Compound statements — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: Parameters before `/` may only be passed positionally and parameters after `*` may only be passed by keyword.

questions.prompt: Explain what `*args` and `**kwargs` collect, and when you would use keyword-only parameters.

model_answer.summary: `*args` gathers extra positional arguments into a tuple and `**kwargs` gathers extra keyword arguments into a dict. Keyword-only parameters force callers to name options, which prevents mistakes caused by argument order.
key_points: `*args` collects extra positional arguments into a tuple
`**kwargs` collects extra keyword arguments into a dict
Parameters after a bare `*` or after `*args` are keyword-only and must be passed by name
Keyword-only parameters make call sites readable and stop callers passing flags or options in the wrong order

questions.explanation: `*args` and `**kwargs` are essential for decorators, which must forward whatever arguments they receive. Keyword-only parameters are good API design for boolean flags and optional settings.

sources.title: 8. Compound statements — Python 3.14.7 documentation
sources.claim: `*identifier` receives a tuple of excess positional arguments, `**identifier` receives a new mapping of excess keyword arguments, and parameters after `*` or `*identifier` are keyword-only.

questions.prompt:
```python
def make_counter():
    count = 0
    def inc():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return inc

c = make_counter()
```
Which of these are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Each call to `c()` starts over from `count = 0` and returns 1
`nonlocal count` would also bind to a module-level `count`
`c.__closure__` holds a cell with the binding for `count`

questions.explanation: `inc` is a closure: its free variable `count` lives in a cell, visible in `c.__closure__` (e), which outlives the call to `make_counter`, so calls return 1, then 2 (a), not 1 each time (b). Without `nonlocal`, assigning `count` makes it local to `inc`, so reading it in `count += 1` before it is bound raises `UnboundLocalError` (c). `nonlocal` only reaches enclosing function scopes; a module-level name needs `global` (d).

sources.title: 3. Data model
sources.claim: A function's `__closure__` is None or a tuple of cells that contain bindings for the function's free variables.

sources.title: 7. Simple statements
sources.claim: `nonlocal` makes identifiers refer to names previously bound in nonlocal scopes, which are the local scopes of enclosing functions, and lets nested code rebind them; if a name isn't bound in any nonlocal scope a SyntaxError is raised.

sources.title: 4. Execution model
sources.claim: A name bound in a block is local to it unless declared nonlocal or global, and if a binding occurs anywhere in a block, all uses of the name in that block refer to the current block, which raises an error when it is used before being bound.

questions.prompt: Given `def call(model, *args, retries=3, **kwargs): ...`, you run `call("m", 1, 2, timeout=5)`. Which of these are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Inside the call, `args` is the tuple `(1, 2)`
Inside the call, `args` is the list `[1, 2]`
`retries` can only be passed by keyword

questions.explanation: `*args` receives a tuple of the excess positional arguments, `(1, 2)` (a), not a list (b), and `**kwargs` receives a new mapping of the excess keyword arguments, `{"timeout": 5}` (c). Parameters after `*args` are keyword-only (d), so in `call("m", 1, 2, 4)` the `4` goes into `args` and `retries` stays `3` (e).

sources.title: 8. Compound statements
sources.claim: `*identifier` is initialized to a tuple receiving any excess positional parameters, `**identifier` to a new ordered mapping receiving any excess keyword arguments, and parameters after `*` or `*identifier` are keyword-only and may only be passed by keyword.
